title: Length-increasing Bruhat multiplication for a reductive group
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a reductive affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]: smooth, connected and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Here unipotent means that all geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful finite-dimensional representation. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq B\subseteq G$, where split means isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$, maximality is among torus subgroups, and $B$ is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup; solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups become trivial. Closed subgroups are as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]; smoothness, connectedness and finite type have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Use the roots $\Phi$, positive roots $\Phi^+$ and simple-root base $\Delta$ of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], and the group $W=N_G(T)(F)/T(F)$ and root reflections $s_\alpha$ of [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization]. The normalizer consists of elements conjugating $T$ to itself after every commutative algebra extension. Let $W_\Delta$ be the subgroup of $W$ generated by $\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}$. For $v\in W_\Delta$, define $\ell(v)$ to be the least length of a word in these generators representing $v$, allowing the empty word. For each $x\in W$ choose any representative $n_x\in N_G(T)(F)$ and put $D_x=B(F)n_xB(F)$. If $\alpha\in\Delta$, $v\in W_\Delta$ and $\ell(s_\alpha v)=\ell(v)+1$, then
$$D_{s_\alpha}D_v=D_{s_\alpha v},$$
where $A C=\{ac:a\in A,\ c\in C\}$ for subsets of $G(F)$. There is no semisimplicity, simply connectedness or characteristic hypothesis. When $\Delta$ is empty the assertion is vacuous.

source.place: Proposition 21.75, printed p.448, length-increasing case of its root-group calculation, with Theorem 21.68, pp.445--446, and Appendix C.11/C.22, pp.610--612. Unlike the existing semisimple simply connected product node, this retains the standing split reductive hypotheses of Section 21h.

proof.text: Put $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}\Phi$ and $V=E\otimes_{\mathbf Q}\mathbf R$. By [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization], $W$ is finite and acts faithfully on $E$, hence on $V$. Choose a basis of $V$ and its ordinary dot product $(\ ,\ )_0$, and set $(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}(wx,wy)_0$. This is bilinear, symmetric, positive definite (the identity summand is positive for $x\ne0$) and $W$-invariant by reindexing. The formula in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] makes $s_a$ an involution with $-1$ line $\mathbf R a$ and fixed hyperplane $\langle x,a^\vee\rangle=0$. Invariance implies these eigenspaces are orthogonal: $(x,a)=(s_ax,s_aa)=-(x,a)$ for fixed $x$. Thus $s_a$ is the orthogonal reflection of the deletion lemma. The base $\Delta$ of the root datum is a rational basis of $E$, hence a real basis of $V$; reducedness and the signed integral expansions of roots persist on extending scalars.

source.place: Appendix C.17--C.21, printed pp.611--612; explicit invariant-inner-product construction.

proof.text: Write $P=\Phi^+$. Then $\Phi=P\sqcup(-P)$. For $a\in\Delta$, the reflection formula changes only the $a$ coefficient in a simple-root expansion. If $\beta\in P\setminus\{a\}$, reducedness implies that some other coefficient of $\beta$ is positive. That coefficient remains positive in $s_a\beta$, which is a root, so its coefficients are all nonnegative. Also $s_a\beta\ne a$, since applying $s_a$ would give $\beta=-a$. Involutivity therefore gives $s_a(P\setminus\{a\})=P\setminus\{a\}$. Together with step 1 this verifies the root-set and sign hypotheses of [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion].

source.place: Appendix C.21--C.22, printed p.612; simple-root coordinate argument.

proof.text: Set $s=s_\alpha$ and $n=\ell(v)$. Reversing a word gives a word for its inverse, since each simple reflection is an involution, so $\ell(v^{-1})=n$ and $\ell((sv)^{-1})=\ell(sv)$. Suppose $v^{-1}\alpha\in-P$. Apply [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion] with $b=\alpha$ to a word of length $n$ for $v^{-1}$, using steps 1--2. It gives $n\ge1$ and a word of length $n-1$ for $v^{-1}s$. Faithfulness on $V$ makes this an equality in $W$, so $\ell(sv)\le n-1$, contradicting the hypothesis $\ell(sv)=n+1$. Since $v^{-1}$ permutes the roots, $v^{-1}\alpha\in P$. This proves only the sign implication needed here; it assumes no Coxeter presentation.

source.place: Appendix C.11/C.22, printed pp.610--612; sign implication supplied explicitly via the existing deletion lemma.

proof.text: For a representative $m$ of $w\in W$ and a root $\beta$, conjugation gives $mU_\beta m^{-1}=U_{w\beta}$. Indeed the conjugate is smooth, connected, closed and normalized by $T$, and on its tangent line $t$ acts with character $\beta(m^{-1}tm)=(w\beta)(t)$; the uniqueness assertion in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] applies. The character action is precisely that of [lem-sfb-weyl-reflection-realization], so this also applies to products and inverses of representatives. Write $H=B(F)$, and take the given representatives $n_s,n_v$. Their product $x=n_sn_v$ represents $sv$ and differs from $n_{sv}$ by an element of $T(F)\subseteq H$, hence $HxH=D_{sv}$. The same argument shows that none of the double cosets depends on the chosen representatives.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(c), printed pp.429--430; Section 21h opening, printed p.446; conjugation and representative independence.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], $B=U\rtimes T$. Order the positive roots with $\alpha$ last. By [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates], every $b\in H$ has the form $b=qut$ with $t\in T(F)$, $u\in U_\alpha(F)$, and $q$ a product of points of the other positive root groups. Step 2 says that $s$ permutes these other roots. Step 4 and their inclusion in $U\subseteq B$ therefore give $n_s q n_s^{-1}\in H$. Also $n_s u n_s^{-1}\in U_{-\alpha}(F)$ and $n_s t n_s^{-1}\in T(F)$. Since $T(F)$ normalizes $U_{-\alpha}(F)$, reorder the latter two factors to obtain $$H n_s H n_v H\subseteq H U_{-\alpha}(F)xH.$$ No subgroup property of the product defining $q$ is used.

source.place: Theorem 21.68(a),(b), Remark 21.69, printed pp.445--446; Proposition 21.75, printed p.448, first reduction in (T3).

proof.text: The root action of $x^{-1}$ sends $-\alpha$ to $v^{-1}s(-\alpha)=v^{-1}\alpha\in P$ by step 3. Thus step 4 gives $x^{-1}U_{-\alpha}(F)x=U_{v^{-1}\alpha}(F)\subseteq H$, where positive-root inclusion is [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates]. Consequently $$D_sD_v=Hn_sHn_vH\subseteq HU_{-\alpha}(F)xH=HxH=D_{sv}.$$ For the reverse inclusion, $x=n_sn_v$ belongs to $D_sD_v$, and this product is invariant under left and right multiplication by $H$ directly from the definitions. Hence it contains $HxH=D_{sv}$. This proves the equality. If $v=1$ the same proof applies (the negative-sign supposition in step 3 is impossible for the empty word). If $\Delta=\varnothing$, no $\alpha$ can be chosen and the assertion is vacuous. All root-group inputs used above hold for reductive groups in every characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 21.75, printed p.448, positive-root case of (T3); both inclusions written out.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 21.68 and Remark 21.69, printed pp.445--446; Proposition 21.75, printed p.448, positive-root calculation; Appendix C.17--C.22, printed pp.611--612. The word-deletion sign implication is expanded explicitly.

Step-by-step checks: Step 1 builds the averaged form, and s_a is the orthogonal reflection because s_a lies in the image of W by weyl-reflection-realization. Step 2 shows by reducedness and simple-root coordinates that s_a sends P∖{a} to itself. Step 3 uses root-sign-word-deletion to get the sign implication ℓ(sv)=ℓ(v)+1 ⇒ v^{-1}α>0; the direction is right and the empty word is handled. Step 4 gets mU_βm^{-1}=U_{wβ} from the uniqueness clause of root-subgroup-parametrizations. It leaves implicit that Ad(m)g_β equals g_{wβ} (Ad(m^{-1}) maps it back, or both are one-dimensional); this is one elementary line and I accepted it. Steps 5–6 are Milne's positive-root branch, with both inclusions and representative independence written out. Edge cases checked: empty Δ, v=1, v=s excluded, GL2 and PGL2 (no simply-connected input), and characteristic 2. The node is not a duplicate of simple-bruhat-double-coset-product, which assumes semisimple simply connected G. All citations are in the same unit, so no tool_uses are needed.
